e: The 50th percentile splits the data in half (50% below, 50% above), which is exactly the median. It is also Q2, the second quartile, because the quartiles sit at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles. The mean equals the median only in symmetrical distributions; with skew they differ.
w: The mean equals the median only when the distribution is symmetrical.
The first quartile (Q1) is the 25th percentile.
The mode is the most frequent value, not the middle one.
k: The 50th percentile, the median and Q2 are the same value.
h: Fifty-fifty split = median.

q: Which path shows bar charts or histograms from the Frequencies window?
o: File → Import Data → Excel → Charts → Histogram
e: Inside the Frequencies dialog (Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Frequencies) there is a Charts button offering bar charts, pie charts and histograms (with an optional normal curve). It is the quick route when you are already running frequencies. Graphs → Chart Builder is the full alternative for any chart type.
w: Compute builds variables; it has no Charts option.
Bivariate correlation has no Charts button; scatterplots come from Chart Builder.
Importing data has nothing to do with charts.
k: Quick charts: Frequencies → Charts (bar, pie, histogram); all charts: Graphs → Chart Builder.

q: Why does the summary say a histogram is used for all test scales?
o: Because there are lots of numbers, and it shows the shape of the distribution
Because test scales are nominal variables, so their categories must be shown
Because pie charts cannot display any numbers or percentages at all
Because test scores have only a few possible values
e: Test-scale scores are numeric with many possible values ('lots of numbers'), so a bar for each value would be unreadable. A histogram groups the values into adjacent ranges and shows the shape of the distribution: symmetrical or skewed, one peak or two, any gaps or outliers. That shape guides which statistics to trust, for example whether the mean is a fair summary.
w: Test scales are scale data, not nominal; nominal categories use bar or pie charts.
Pie charts can show numbers; they are simply the wrong tool for many continuous values.
Test scores have many possible values; that is exactly why a histogram is needed.
k: Scale data with many values → histogram, to see the shape of the distribution.
h: Lots of numbers → bins → histogram.

q: A histogram of exam scores is skewed to the LEFT. This means:
e: Left (negative) skew means the long tail stretches toward the low scores while most scores pile up at the high end: more high scores, as with an easy exam where most students do well and a few do badly. Name the skew after the tail, not after the bulk. In left skew the mean is usually below the median, because the low tail pulls it down.
w: More low scores with a tail to the right is right (positive) skew.
Evenly distributed scores describe a symmetrical distribution.
Skew says nothing about outliers being absent; the tail may contain some.
k: Left (negative) skew: tail to the left, most scores high; mean usually below median.
h: Tail on the left, crowd on the right.

q: In a boxplot, how do you recognise an outlier?
o: It is the line in the middle of the box
It is the top edge of the box
e: In a boxplot, any value that appears outside the whiskers is an outlier, plotted individually as a circle (mild) or asterisk (extreme) with its case number. Inside the plot, the box spans Q1 to Q3 (the middle 50%), the line inside the box is the median, and the whiskers reach to the most extreme values that are not outliers.
w: Values inside the box are the middle 50% of the data, not outliers.
The line in the middle of the box is the median.
The top edge of the box is Q3, the 75th percentile.
k: Outliers are the points beyond the whiskers (° mild, * extreme), labelled with case numbers.
h: Whiskers are the fence; anything outside is an outlier.

q: Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 30. Below which value does a LOW score become a mild outlier?
e: The fences are symmetrical around the box. IQR = 30 − 20 = 10, and 1.5 × IQR = 15. The low mild fence is Q1 − 15 = 20 − 15 = 5, so scores below 5 are at least mild outliers. The low extreme fence is Q1 − 3 × IQR = 20 − 30 = −10. Low fences subtract from Q1; high fences add to Q3.
w: 10 is Q1 − IQR, one box-length; the rule uses 1.5 box-lengths.
15 is Q1 − 0.5 × IQR, too close to the box.
−10 is the extreme fence (Q1 − 3 × IQR), not the mild one.
k: Low fences: mild = Q1 − 1.5 × IQR; extreme = Q1 − 3 × IQR.
h: Same rule, opposite side: subtract from Q1.

q: How does SPSS help you find an outlier in the dataset?
o: Each outlier is labelled with its case (row) number
It deletes the outliers automatically from the Data View
It colours the outlier's whole column red in Variable View
e: SPSS labels each outlier in a boxplot with its case (row) number, so you can go straight to that row in Data View, check the raw value, and decide whether it is a typing error to correct or a genuine extreme score to keep. SPSS never deletes outliers automatically; that decision is always the researcher's.
w: SPSS never deletes data automatically; it labels each outlier with its row number so you can decide.
SPSS has no feature that colours outlier columns in Variable View.
Compute creates variables; it doesn't list outliers.
k: SPSS boxplots label each outlier with its case number so you can find and check it.

q: The same patients complete the PHQ-9 before and after 12 sessions of CBT. Which test compares the two means?
e: The same patients measured before and after treatment produce paired scores: each patient's 'after' is linked to their own 'before'. The paired-samples t-test analyses the before–after differences, which removes stable differences between patients and gives more power. The summary's own example is exactly this: the same participants before and after a psychotherapy intervention.
w: Independent-samples is for two separate groups of people.
One-sample compares one mean with a fixed value.
Chi-square relates categorical variables; PHQ-9 totals are scores.
k: Before and after in the same people → paired-samples t-test.
h: Same patients, two times = a pair.

q: Match test to question: (1) Does mean anxiety differ between 4 age groups? (2) Is marital status related to diagnosis category? (3) Does hours of sleep predict mood score?
o: (1) Independent t-test; (2) Crosstabs only; (3) Paired t-test
e: Match the question to the data. (1) Mean anxiety, a numeric outcome, across four groups calls for ANOVA. (2) Marital status by diagnosis category is two categorical variables, so chi-square. (3) Hours of sleep predicting mood score is one numeric variable predicting another, so regression (correlation would only describe the association; 'predict' signals regression).
w: Chi-square cannot compare means, ANOVA cannot relate two categorical variables, and 'predict' calls for regression.
A t-test compares only two groups, and a paired t-test doesn't predict one variable from another.
Pearson correlation needs numeric variables, and a one-sample t-test doesn't predict anything.
k: Means of 3+ groups → ANOVA; two categorical variables → chi-square; predict one variable from another → regression.
h: Means → ANOVA, Categories → Chi-square, Predict → Regression.

q: Why can't chi-square be used to compare mean IQ between two groups?
o: Chi-square is for categorical variables, not numeric means
Chi-square only works when there are three or more groups
Chi-square requires a known population mean such as 100
e: Chi-square works on counts in categories: it asks whether the distribution of one categorical variable depends on another. IQ is a numeric score, and the question is about means, so the right test is the independent-samples t-test. The summary puts it plainly: chi-square is for categorical variables, not numeric ones.
w: Chi-square works with two or more categories; group count isn't the issue.
A known population mean is what a one-sample t-test uses.
Chi-square assumes independent observations; paired data need a different test.
k: Numeric means → t-test or ANOVA; categorical counts → chi-square.
h: Chi-square counts; t-tests average.

q: A t-test is used to:
o: Compare means to see if a difference is significant
Compare two categorical variables in a crosstab table
Show the shape of a distribution and its skewness
Count how often each value appears in a variable
e: A t-test compares means and checks whether the difference between them is statistically significant, that is, larger than you would expect from sampling variation alone. There are three versions: one-sample (one mean versus a known value), paired-samples (the same people twice) and independent-samples (two separate groups). For three or more means, use ANOVA.
w: Comparing two categorical variables is a job for crosstabs and chi-square.
The shape of a distribution is shown by a histogram and skewness statistics.
Counting how often each value appears is Frequencies.
k: t-test = compare two means (or one mean with a value) for a significant difference.
h: t for 'two': two means at most.

q: Pearson r = 0.04 with Sig = 0.71. Conclusion?
o: No meaningful correlation, and not significant
e: Read both numbers. r = 0.04 is almost zero, so there is essentially no linear relationship. Sig = 0.71 is far above 0.05, so the result is not significant (in the course's terms, accept H₀). Both agree: no meaningful correlation. Remember that r measures only straight-line association, so a scatterplot could still reveal a curved pattern.
w: r = 0.04 is close to zero, not strong, and 0.71 is not significant.
r is positive and tiny, not strongly negative, and not significant.
A p-value above 0.05 means not significant.
k: r near 0 and p > .05 → no meaningful, significant correlation.

q: In the model answer for r = 0.958, Sig = 0.001, what does 'significant' mean?
o: The correlation is very unlikely to have happened by chance
The correlation is perfect, so r must equal exactly 1
Working hours cause salary to rise, which the test proves
95% of the data lie on a straight line
e: 'Significant' here means the correlation is very unlikely to have happened by chance if there were really no relationship: Sig = 0.001 is far below 0.05. It is a statement about evidence, not about size or cause. A correlation can be significant but small in a big sample, and even a strong, significant correlation does not prove causation.
w: Significance doesn't mean perfect; r = 0.958 is strong but not 1.
Correlation does not prove causation, however significant.
Significance is not the percentage of points on a line.
k: Significant = unlikely to be due to chance alone; it says nothing about cause and nothing about size by itself.
h: Significant means 'probably real', not 'large' or 'causal'.

q: In the IQ table, Sig. (2-tailed) = .018. What is the decision?
o: Significant (.018 < .05) → reject H₀ and accept H₁
Significant only if t is negative
Undecided, because the CI must be checked first
e: Sig. is SPSS's name for the p-value. .018 ≤ .05, so the difference between the sample mean IQ and 100 is statistically significant: reject H₀ and accept H₁. It agrees with the critical-value check (|t| = 2.964 > 2.306) and with the CI of the difference, which excludes 0. All three routes give the same decision.
w: Not significant would require p > .05; .018 is smaller.
Significance does not depend on the sign of t; the sign only gives direction.
No extra check is needed; p alone decides, and the CI agrees anyway.
k: Sig. ≤ .05 → significant → reject H₀ (accept H₁); the CI and critical t agree.
h: Sig. is SPSS's nickname for p.

q: If the same table had shown t = −2.964 (same df and p), what would you conclude?
o: Significant, and the sample mean IQ is lower than 100
Not significant, because t is negative
Significant, and the sample mean is higher than 100
e: Significance depends on the size of t (|t| = 2.964 > 2.306) or on p, not on its sign, so the result would still be significant. The sign gives the direction: a negative t means the sample mean is below the test value. The conclusion would be that the sample's mean IQ is significantly lower than 100, and the mean difference and its CI would also be negative.
w: A negative t can be significant; significance depends on |t| or p.
Negative t means below the test value, not above it.
Negative t values are perfectly valid; they just indicate direction.
k: For t: the size (|t| or p) decides significance; the sign decides direction.
h: Size says 'is it real?', sign says 'which way?'

q: Why does the 95% CI of the difference (1.53 to 12.25) agree with p = .018?
o: Because the interval does not contain 0
Because the interval is wider than df
e: A 95% CI of the difference contains the plausible values of the true difference. If 0 (no difference) lies outside the interval, 'no difference' is not plausible at the 5% level, which is the same decision as p < .05. Here the whole interval, 1.53 to 12.25, is above 0, so it agrees with p = .018. If the interval had included 0, p would be above .05.
w: 100 is the test value; the CI of the difference is compared with 0, not 100.
Comparing an interval limit with t has no meaning.
Comparing a CI's width with df has no meaning.
k: 95% CI of a difference excludes 0 ⇔ p < .05 (two-tailed).
h: Zero outside the net = significant.

q: What does the 'Test Value = 100' in the One-Sample Test table represent?
o: The known population mean the sample is compared with (worldwide mean IQ)
The sample mean IQ obtained from the nine participants in the study
The critical value of t that the result must exceed to be significant
e: The test value is the fixed number the sample mean is compared with: here the normal worldwide mean IQ of 100, entered in the dialog's 'Test Value' box. H₀ says the population mean equals 100. SPSS then reports the mean difference (sample mean − 100), t, df, Sig. and a CI for that difference.
w: The sample mean is 106.889; the test value is the comparison point.
The critical t (2.306) comes from tables, not from the Test Value box.

q: Degrees of freedom are defined in the course as:
o: The number of values that are free to vary
The probability the result is due to chance
The range of the middle 50% of data
e: Degrees of freedom are the number of values that are free to vary once something has been fixed. If 5 scores must have a mean of 10, you can choose any 4 freely, but the fifth is then forced, so df = 4 (n − 1). df determines which t (or F, or χ²) distribution is used, and therefore the critical value: fewer df give heavier tails and stricter cutoffs.
w: The cutoff that decides significance is the critical value.
The probability of the result under H₀ is the p-value.
The range of the middle 50% is the IQR.
k: df = the number of values free to vary (one-sample t: n − 1); df sets the critical value.
h: Five friends, fixed bill: four choose freely, the last pays what's left.

q: Descriptive statistics:
o: Describe the data with numbers such as mean, median and SD
Test whether group differences are statistically significant
Predict one variable from another using a regression line
e: Descriptive statistics summarize the data you have: centre (mean, median, mode), spread (SD, variance, range) and position (percentiles). They do not test hypotheses or generalize beyond the sample; that is the job of inferential statistics (t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square, correlation tests, regression), which use p-values and CIs to infer something about the population.
w: Testing whether differences are statistically significant is inferential statistics, not descriptive.
Prediction with a regression line is inferential or modelling statistics.
Recoding values into categories is a data transformation step, not a way of describing data.
k: Descriptive statistics describe the sample (centre, spread, position); inferential statistics test and generalize.
h: Describe what you have; infer what you don't.

q: According to the course, what does a confidence interval estimate?
o: The range likely to contain the true population mean
The range that contains every participant's score
The probability that H₀ is true
The spread between Q1 and Q3
e: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter, here the true population mean: 'the actual average of a variable for the entire population, not just your sample'. A 95% CI (for example 45–55) comes from a method that captures the true mean in 95% of samples. It is about the population mean, not about individual scores.
w: A CI is about the population mean, not the range of every participant's score.
A CI says nothing about the probability that H₀ is true.
The spread between Q1 and Q3 is the IQR.
k: A CI is a range of plausible values for the population parameter (e.g., the true mean).
h: A CI is a net cast to catch the true population mean.
